newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani stocks seen up 23 percent by mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani stocks seen up 23 percent by mid-1997.

text.p: Pakistani stocks are likely to improve about 23 percent by mid-1997 once political and economic uncertainties have subsided, brokerage house ING Baring Securities said on Wednesday.
"We continue to recommend a buy on the market with a one-year view and a target return of 20 to 21 percent in dollar terms," Kalim Aziz, research head at Baring, wrote in a report.

Aziz said the Karachi market could remain volatile in November and December because of uncertainty resulting from the November 5 dismissal of Benazir Bhutto's government, but he said the market's performance would improve in the first and second quarters.
"Our target for first half 1997 is 1,850 points," he said.
The 100-share index jumped over the 1,500-point mark early on Wednesday afternoon, buoyed by hopes that talks with International Monetary Fund (IMF) officials would lead to a resumption of lending.
The market gained 6.71 points to close at 1,486.21 on Tuesday after losing ground in several sessions.
The index fluctuated wildly after President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto on charges of corruption and misrule and installed an interim government to supervise elections set for February 3.
The market celebrated Bhutto's removal with a 78-point jump, but sank 70 points the next day after Moody's Investors Service cut Pakistan's credit ratings.
"The volatile market movements have taken place in a period of rapid change," Aziz said, adding that the government, the economic scenario and public attitudes had all changed.
Aziz agreed with market perceptions that the caretaker government had yet to clarify its plan of action.
"We do not expect miracles from the interim government," he said but added: "We firmly believe that there is an improvement over the past."
He said changes introduced by the caretaker government were likely to survive the transition to an elected government in February and said international lending agencies would support them.
IMF Middle East director Paul Chabrier arrived in Islamabad on Wednesday to try to reach agreement on a letter of intent for the release of delayed tranches of a $600 million standby loan.
Dealers said major investors would wait for a final word on the outcome of the talks before taking fresh positions.
"We expect that some of the ambiguities will be sorted out by the end of the current year," Aziz said.
